title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
This page sits inside Theorem §28 of E449, which claims that x^n − 1 ≡ 0 (mod P), with P prime and 0 < x < P, has at most n solutions.

(i) The case n = 3. Since x^3 − 1 = (x − 1)(x^2 + x + 1), and P is prime, either x ≡ 1 or x^2 + x + 1 ≡ 0. If a is a root of x^2 + x + 1 ≡ 0, then so is a^2, because a^3 ≡ 1 and higher powers of a reduce to earlier ones. Suppose b is another root. Subtracting the two congruences gives (a − b)(a + b + 1) ≡ 0. So either b ≡ a, or b ≡ −1 − a. In the second case, using a^2 + a + 1 ≡ 0 gives a^2 − b ≡ 0, so b ≡ a^2. Hence there are at most three residues: 1, a, a^2.

(ii) The general case. If a is a root, then x^n − 1 = (x − a)Q(x) + (a^n − 1), and the remainder a^n − 1 is divisible by P. So (x − a)Q(x) ≡ 0. By primality, any other root b ≢ a must be a root of Q, which has degree n − 1. Iterating, as in the theory of equations, there are at most n roots. This is the factor-theorem proof that a polynomial has at most deg-many roots modulo a prime, specialised to x^n − 1.

(iii) Euler then lists the roots as 1, a, a^2, …, a^{n−1}, 'since a^n is again equivalent to unity'.

Purpose: this bound is the tool Euler uses later in E449 for counting 'proper' cases (§30, roots of exact order n) and for his attempted existence proof of primitive roots.
errors: The final list x = 1, a, a^2, …, a^{n−1} is the full root set only if a has exact multiplicative order n mod P. If a has smaller order d (for example a = 1), the list repeats and contains only d distinct values. If n does not divide P − 1, no element of order n exists. The Scholion (§29) partly concedes the second point ('quasi imaginarii' cases), but the list as stated is inaccurate.
Minor gap in (i): the step from P | (a − b)(a + b + 1) to 'P divides one factor' uses Euclid's lemma tacitly. This is standard and harmless.
Degenerate case P = 3 in (i): a = 1 = a^2, so the 'three cases' coincide. This is consistent with 'at most', but goes unremarked.

ideas.what: A polynomial congruence (here x^n − 1) modulo a prime has at most n roots, proved by repeatedly splitting off a linear factor (x − a) and using primality.
ideas.modern_name: Lagrange's theorem on polynomial congruences (at most deg f roots over F_p)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1768, published 1770); used earlier, or in parallel, by Euler for x^n − 1
ideas.where_published: E449 itself (Novi Comment. 18, 1774). A similar argument appears to occur in Euler's Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (E792, posthumous), but I am unsure of the details.

ideas.what: Explicit handling of x^2 + x + 1 ≡ 0: if a is a root then the other root is −1 − a ≡ a^2.
ideas.modern_name: Vieta relation for the roots of the cyclotomic polynomial Φ3 mod p (cube roots of unity)

ideas.what: If a is a root of x^n ≡ 1, then all powers of a are roots, so the roots form a cyclic family generated by an element of order n.
ideas.modern_name: Subgroup of n-th roots of unity in (Z/p)^*; cyclic when n | p − 1

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard, well-documented piece of Euler's work on residues. The root-count bound is well known and attributed to Lagrange and Euler. The only notable feature is the small inaccuracy in the root list, which is already implicitly qualified in the Scholion.
